reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Neurocutaneous Disorders (current reference texts)
clinicalPearls: A rare mosaic neurocutaneous disorder defined by the triad of cutaneous, ocular and central nervous system lipomatous and malformative lesions
The hallmark skin lesion is the naevus psiloparakeratoticus (naevus psiloliparus), a hairless fatty naevus of the scalp, often with overlying alopecia
It is caused by post-zygotic activating variants in the RAS pathway, chiefly FGFR1 and sometimes KRAS, so lesions are segmental
The characteristic ocular lesion is an epibulbar (limbal) dermoid or lipodermoid choristoma
Central nervous system features include intracranial and intraspinal lipomas, arachnoid cysts, cortical malformations and, occasionally, low-grade glioma
Neurological presentation may include seizures, developmental delay and, uncommonly, tumour formation, so imaging surveillance is important
Management is generic and multidisciplinary: antiseizure therapy, surgery for symptomatic lipomas or cysts, and ophthalmological and developmental support
reference.pathophysiology: Encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis is a mosaic RASopathy caused by a post-zygotic activating variant, most often in FGFR1 and occasionally KRAS, arising early in embryogenesis and affecting neuroectodermal and mesodermal lineages. The resulting clone produces abnormal adipose overgrowth and malformation across the skin, eye and central nervous system, giving the characteristic scalp naevus psiloliparus, epibulbar choristomas and intracranial or intraspinal lipomas. Cortical malformations and arachnoid cysts arise from disturbed neural development, and the persistent RAS-pathway activation underlies the occasional occurrence of low-grade central nervous system tumours in affected individuals.
additionalDifferentials: Aplasia cutis congenita of the scalp
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy of the scalp naevus where diagnosis is uncertain
MRI of the brain and spine to detect lipomas, arachnoid cysts and cortical malformations
Ophthalmological assessment for epibulbar dermoid or lipodermoid
MRA where an associated vascular anomaly is suspected
Molecular analysis of affected tissue for FGFR1/KRAS variants where available
redFlags: Progressive neurological deficit or developmental regression
Imaging features suggesting an evolving central nervous system tumour
Compressive symptoms from an intraspinal or intracranial lipoma
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is variable and depends on the extent of central nervous system involvement; many patients have stable disease with manageable seizures, but extensive cortical malformation, large lipomas or tumour development is associated with greater neurological morbidity.
pitfalls: Mistaking the scalp naevus for isolated aplasia cutis and not screening for CNS and ocular disease
Overlooking an epibulbar choristoma on cursory eye examination
Failing to arrange spinal imaging when only cranial disease is apparent
Not maintaining surveillance for the small risk of low-grade tumour
references: Happle R. Mosaicism in Human Skin
